summary: Muslims, a majority of residents, follow faraid: fixed shares to heirs and at most one third by will. Non-Muslims can leave their estate freely and dependants may apply to court for provision. The Hague Trusts Convention is not in force, but Malaysia has trust law and Labuan offers a private foundation.
reserved_share: Muslims: faraid fixed shares; a wasiat (will) may dispose of at most one third to non-heirs unless the heirs consent (state Syariah enactments and the Administration of Islamic Law Acts).
family_claims: Non-Muslims: freedom of testation under the Wills Act 1959, with family provision under the Inheritance (Family Provision) Act 1971; intestacy under the Distribution Act 1958.
foreign_law_note: Non-Muslims: common-law rules, movables follow the law of domicile and land follows Malaysian law. Muslims cannot opt out of Islamic law. Sabah and Sarawak have their own native-custom rules. I did not source the conflict rule in a statute.
trust_note: Not on the HCCH status table. Trusts: Trustee Act 1949 and the Labuan Trusts Act 1996; Muslims often use waqf and hibah. Onshore there is no private foundation, only charitable bodies. The Labuan Foundations Act 2010 allows foundations in Labuan, including for non-charitable purposes. No inheritance tax applies.
open_questions: Confirm the Inheritance (Family Provision) Act 1971 and the Labuan Foundations Act 2010 details; neither was retrieved.
